newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Skanska sells Sandvik stake in reshuffle.
newsitem.headline: Skanska sells Sandvik stake in reshuffle.

text.p: Leading Swedish construction group Skanska said on Monday it was selling its entire stake in tool maker/engineer Sandvik which analysts saw as part of the current powermongering in the industrial sector.

Skanska, the biggest shareholder in Sandvik with 20 percent of capital and 25 percent of votes, said it was selling over half of its 10 billion crown holding to Swedish investor Industrivarden and Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
Skanska said it would also guarantee a Sandvik share redemption programme worth four billion crowns, pledging 23.5 million Sandvik shares and so fully subscribing the offer.

The sale, first mooted in 1993, came as Percy Barnevik leaves Skanska's chairmanship to head Investor, the investment arm of Sweden's powerful Wallenberg family that is reorganising the leadership of its massive empire.

Skanska falls under the Handelsbanken circle which is Swedish business's second power house, rivalling the Wallenbergs, with Industrivarden, investors Custos, Oresund, and Latour and businessmen Mats Hagstromer and Sven Quiberg linked into that sphere.
"The fact that Barnevik is leaving the board this week was a signal there would be change," said one Stockholm analyst.
"Barnevik is chairman of Sandvik with links with that company since 1969 and he wanted to make sure it had a new long term owner. Industrivarden will be this."
Industrivarden will buy 22 million Sandvik A-series shares at 185 crowns each, an investment of 4.1 billion crowns, which amounts to 10.2 percent of votes and 7.9 percent of capital.
Deutsche Morgan Grenfell (DMG) will buy 10 million A-series shares at 180 crowns each, to sell to institutional investors in Sweden and internationally.
With Barnevik leaving, Skanska said current chief executive (CEO) Melker Schorling would become chairman and head of Skanska's U.S. operations, Claes Bjork, become CEO.

"I think it is rather positive for Skanska as they will streamline the company's structure, moving away from being a holding company to focus on construction and property," Fiba analyst Jan Dworsky told Reuters.
Skanska shares rose six crowns to 330 crowns on Monday morning while Sandvik's B-series shares slipped 6.5 to 187 crowns and its A shares fell 7.5 to 185.5 crowns.
The divestment was not a surprise to the markets. Skanska told the markets in 1993 it intended to sell its Sandvik stake as part of a process to focus on core operations.
Skanska has also made clear that it wants to sell its 8.7 percent stake of capital in bearings manufacturer SKF.
Skanska said the sale of its Sandvik stake would give the company a capital gain of 9.1 billion crowns but did not say how it would use these funds.
Analysts said the deal was neutral for Sandvik, with one strong long term owner replacing another, but it would be interesting to see where the 10 million DMG shares went.
"Sandvik is one of the blue chip companies with the least ownership by international institutions so it is likely that they will get a fair share of the placing," Dworsky said.
"The company is attractive, a market leader in its industry that is profitable, with a strong balance sheet...one of Sweden's highest quality companies."

Sandvik said the share redemption programme, which will be priced at a three percent discount to the market, was designed to improve its capital structure and create possibilities for increased shareholder value.
